Peritoneal, retroperitoneal and extraperitoneal spaces

Explore the abdominal and pelvic compartments on a real CT, with every space outlined in color and an atlas-style painted plate of every slice, and on a labeled teaching phantom in 3D linked to axial, coronal and sagittal images. Pour fluid, blood, urine, pus or gas into a space and watch where it goes, place masses and work out where they come from, then score peritoneal disease.

Compartment map

Three compartments and one connecting system. The peritoneal cavity is a potential space lined by peritoneum. The retroperitoneum behind it is divided by the renal fascia into the anterior pararenal, perirenal and posterior pararenal spaces, with the great vessels in the middle. The extraperitoneal pelvis continues the retroperitoneum downward around the bladder and rectum and up the anterior abdominal wall. Joining all of them is the subperitoneal space: the fat inside the ligaments and mesenteries, which carries vessels, lymphatics and nerves, and disease, between organs.

Peritoneal cavity

The transverse mesocolon divides it into supramesocolic and inframesocolic compartments. The small bowel mesentery splits the inframesocolic space into a closed right triangle and a left space that opens into the pelvis.

Where fluid pools

Supine, the most dependent sites are the pelvis and, in the upper abdomen, the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch). The right paracolic gutter is wide and links them; the left is narrower and the phrenicocolic ligament partly closes it above.

Lesser sac

Behind the stomach and lesser omentum, in front of the pancreas. Its only opening is the foramen of Winslow behind the hepatoduodenal ligament, so fluid confined here points to a neighbor: the pancreas or a posterior gastric ulcer.

Why?

Retroperitoneum

Anterior pararenal space: pancreas, duodenum and the ascending and descending colon, continuous across the midline. Perirenal space: kidney, adrenal and proximal ureter inside the renal fascia. Posterior pararenal space: only fat. The great vessel space sits between the two perirenal spaces.

Why?

Interfascial planes

The renal fascia is laminated. Fluid under pressure, such as pancreatic fluid or blood, dissects between its layers in the retromesenteric, retrorenal and lateroconal planes. These planes connect the spaces with each other and with the pelvis, so the three spaces are not sealed boxes.

Why?

Routes out of the abdomen

Upward, the retrocrural space around the aorta continues through the aortic hiatus into the posterior mediastinum. Downward, the retroperitoneum continues into the pelvic sidewall, the groin and, along the psoas, the thigh. Anteriorly, the properitoneal fat links the flank with the prevesical space.

Subperitoneal space and the mesentery as one organ

Ligaments and mesenteries are continuous with each other and with the retroperitoneum: the transverse mesocolon root lies across the pancreas, and the small bowel mesentery root starts at the duodenojejunal flexure. Pancreatitis, tumors and lymphatic disease travel along this single connected organ.

Why?

Where will it go?

Load a scenario and press Play under the images. The simulation fills the source space first and spreads along the open routes. Fluid runs to dependent recesses, gas rises, and crossing a fascial layer takes pressure. Switch the patient to upright to see fluid fall into the pelvis. Watch the volume slider: a small leak stays local, a large one reaches distant spaces.

Peritoneal fluid and blood

Fluid fills the pelvis, climbs the right gutter to Morison pouch and reaches the right subphrenic space. In hemoperitoneum, the densest clot lies next to the bleeding organ: the sentinel clot. Active extravasation is contrast-dense blood that grows between phases.

Gas: where it is tells you what perforated

Free intraperitoneal gas rises to the front of the liver and under the anterior wall, and moves with position. Retroperitoneal gas outlines the kidney, duodenum or psoas, does not move, and can track up into the mediastinum. Use the lung window.

Retroperitoneal fluid

Pancreatitis fills the anterior pararenal space on both sides and runs into the mesocolon and mesentery. Perirenal blood stays inside the renal fascia and descends in the cone. A ruptured aortic aneurysm bleeds around the aorta into the posterior pararenal and left perirenal spaces.

Into the chest

Fluid and gas cross the diaphragm behind the crura and through the aortic and esophageal hiatuses. A mediastinal collection in a patient with pancreatitis is a pancreatic pseudocyst until proven otherwise.

FindingWhat it suggestsWhere to look
Sentinel clotClot of higher attenuation (often about 45 to 70 HU) next to the source of bleedingAround the organ suspected to bleed, compared with lower-density blood further away
Hematocrit levelLayering blood: coagulopathy or anticoagulation, or bleeding of some hoursDependent part of a collection
Active extravasationOngoing bleeding: contrast-dense blood that changes shape and grows between arterial, portal and delayed phasesCompare phases at the same level
Free gas anterior to the liverIntraperitoneal perforation (stomach, duodenal bulb, colon)Lung window, under the anterior abdominal wall
Gas around the right kidney and duodenumRetroperitoneal duodenal perforation (after ERCP, trauma)Right anterior pararenal and perirenal spaces
Contrast-dense urine outside the collecting systemForniceal rupture or ureteral injuryDelayed excretory phase

How disease spreads

Disease travels by four routes: direct invasion, seeding across the peritoneal cavity, lymphatic spread and spread through blood vessels. The subperitoneal space carries the first and the third: tumor, inflammation and lymphatics run along the ligaments and mesenteries from one organ to the next, without ever crossing the peritoneal cavity.

Subperitoneal spread

Follow the vessels in the ligament. Gastric cancer runs along the left gastric vessels in the gastrohepatic ligament; pancreatic cancer reaches the transverse colon through the mesocolon and the small bowel through the mesentery root; colon cancer travels the same roads in reverse.

Why?

Seeding follows the fluid

Cells shed into the peritoneal fluid settle where it pools and where it is absorbed: the pouch of Douglas, the right lower quadrant at the end of the mesentery root, the upper border of the sigmoid mesocolon, the right paracolic gutter, Morison pouch, under the right hemidiaphragm and in the greater omentum.

Peritoneal cancer index

Nine abdominopelvic regions (0 to 8) and four small bowel regions (9 to 12) each receive the size of their largest lesion: 0 none, 1 up to 0.5 cm, 2 up to 5 cm, 3 larger or confluent. The total runs from 0 to 39. CT misses many implants smaller than 5 mm, especially on the small bowel and its mesentery, so CT tends to underestimate it.

What changes the operation

  • Small bowel serosa and the mesentery root: diffuse disease there usually prevents complete cytoreduction.
  • Hepatoduodenal ligament and porta hepatis, lesser sac and gastrohepatic ligament.
  • Ureters and pelvic sidewall; the diaphragm (resectable but laborious).
  • Ascites volume and omental cake.

Pelvis and wall

Below the peritoneal reflection the spaces are extraperitoneal. The prevesical space of Retzius lies in front of the bladder and continues up the anterior abdominal wall; the perivesical, mesorectal and presacral spaces surround the pelvic organs; the sidewall connects with the retroperitoneum, the groin and the thigh.

Bladder rupture at CT cystography

Extraperitoneal (most common, usually with pelvic fractures): contrast fills the prevesical space around the bladder, the molar tooth, and can extend up the wall, into the thigh or the scrotum. Usually managed with a catheter. Intraperitoneal (a blow to a full bladder): contrast outlines bowel loops and the paracolic gutters; needs surgical repair.

Rectus sheath hematoma and the arcuate line

Above the arcuate line, about a third of the way from the umbilicus to the pubis, the posterior sheath confines the hematoma to one side. Below it, only the transversalis fascia lies behind the muscle, so blood enters the prevesical space, crosses the midline and can indent the bladder.

Presacral space

Between the mesorectal fascia and the sacrum, normally about 1 to 1.5 cm or less. Widening means fluid, blood or a mass. Group the masses by origin: congenital, neurogenic, osseous, fatty or hematopoietic, inflammatory.

Mesorectal fascia

The envelope of the mesorectum and the circumferential resection margin plane for rectal cancer. Fluid inside it (an anastomotic leak, a perforation) stays outlined by the fascia until it is breached.

Where is this mass from?

Decide first whether the mass arises from an organ or is a primary retroperitoneal tumor, because the differential and the biopsy route depend on it. Then use the compartment: a mass in the perirenal space is usually renal or adrenal, one in the great vessel space is nodal or vascular, and one along the spine is neurogenic.

SignMeaningTry it
Claw (beak) signThe organ's edge wraps around the mass: it arises from that organ
Embedded organAn organ that cannot be separated from the mass and is deformed by it (often a vessel) is the likely origin
Phantom (invisible) organA normal organ is missing from its place and the mass sits there
Prominent feeding arteryThe artery that feeds the mass points to its origin
Displacement without a clawA fat plane or smooth displacement of neighbors: primary retroperitoneal mass
Encasement without narrowingSoft tissue around the vessels, lifting the aorta: lymphoma. Anterior plaque sparing the back: fibrosis
Along a nerveFusiform mass in the psoas or paravertebral region, foraminal widening

Before the needle

  • Suspected retroperitoneal sarcoma: core biopsy through a retroperitoneal (posterior) route, avoiding the peritoneal cavity, after review at a sarcoma center.
  • Possible paraganglioma: check plasma or urine metanephrines first.
  • Presacral cyst: exclude an anterior meningocele before any transrectal or transvaginal drainage.
  • Fat-containing tumor: biopsy the non-fatty nodule, which carries the grade.

Practice

An unnamed tumor appears in the viewer; scroll through it in all three planes and choose its origin. Your score is kept.

Composition

After location, composition narrows the list. Change the phase or the MRI sequence in the bar above the images while each mass is loaded.

ComponentHow it looksThink ofTry it
Macroscopic fatBelow about −50 HU, bright on T1, drops with fat suppressionLiposarcoma, angiomyolipoma, myelolipoma, teratoma, extramedullary hematopoiesis
Myxoid matrixNear water on CT, very bright on T2, slow reticular enhancementMyxoid liposarcoma, neurogenic tumors, myxoma
CysticWater attenuation; check the wall, septa and nodulesLymphangioma, tailgut cyst, duplication cyst, meningocele, cystic neurogenic tumor
HypervascularAvid arterial enhancementParaganglioma, hypervascular metastasis, Castleman disease, hemangiopericytoma
Homogeneous soft tissueMild uniform enhancement, encases vesselsLymphoma, retroperitoneal fibrosis
NecrosisEnhancing rim with non-enhancing centerLeiomyosarcoma, adrenal carcinoma, high-grade sarcoma
Delayed enhancement and whorlsLow attenuation that enhances slowly; whorled on T2Ganglioneuroma
CalcificationDense foci on non-contrast CTAdrenal carcinoma, neuroblastoma, teratoma, chordoma (bone fragments)

Mimics and pseudotumors

Before calling a mass, ask whether it is bowel, a vessel, a normal variant or an inflammatory process. Scrolling through it in several planes and comparing its enhancement with the nearby organs solves most of them.

Pseudotumors in the model

Each loads into the viewer with its clues. Change the phase to compare the lesion with the spleen, the veins or the bowel wall.

Variants that look like masses

A left or duplicated IVC mimics a left para-aortic node; azygos continuation mimics retrocrural nodes; a retroaortic left renal vein can look like a nodule behind the aorta; a pelvic kidney can look like a pelvic mass.

Why? (IVC)Why? (kidney)
Mimic of carcinomatosisClues
Tuberculous peritonitisHigh-attenuation ascites, smooth peritoneal thickening, low-attenuation (necrotic) nodes, omental and mesenteric involvement
Peritoneal lymphomatosisBulky lymphadenopathy, homogeneous soft tissue, bowel wall thickening without obstruction
Malignant peritoneal mesotheliomaSheet-like peritoneal masses, often with relatively little ascites; asbestos exposure and pleural plaques in some
SplenosisPrior splenic trauma or splenectomy; nodules that match spleen on every phase; heat-damaged red blood cell scan confirms
EndometriosisPelvic predominance, T1-bright hemorrhagic foci on MRI, cyclic symptoms
Leiomyomatosis peritonealis disseminataMultiple smooth-muscle nodules, usually in women of reproductive age, often with uterine fibroids
Sclerosing encapsulating peritonitisLong-term peritoneal dialysis; a thick membrane cocoons clustered small bowel loops, often calcified

Peritoneal fossae and internal hernias

An internal hernia is bowel passing through a normal or abnormal opening inside the peritoneal cavity. Congenital ones use fossae that remain where fusion was incomplete (paraduodenal, foramen of Winslow, pericecal, intersigmoid); postoperative ones use defects created by surgery and are now the most common in adults.

Paraduodenal hernias

Left (fossa of Landzert): a sac of jejunum left of the duodenojejunal flexure with the inferior mesenteric vein in its front wall. Right (fossa of Waldeyer): small bowel trapped behind the superior mesenteric vessels in the right mesocolon, linked to nonrotation.

Why?

Foramen of Winslow and transmesenteric

Through the foramen, bowel enters the lesser sac behind the hepatoduodenal ligament. Through a mesenteric defect, loops lie lateral to the colon without a sac, after Roux-en-Y reconstruction, liver transplantation or in children.

Why?

Signs common to all

  • A cluster or sac of small bowel loops in an unusual place
  • Crowded, stretched and engorged mesenteric vessels converging on the hernia neck; a whirl at the defect
  • Displacement of a landmark vessel (inferior mesenteric vein, superior mesenteric vessels)
  • Small bowel obstruction, closed-loop signs and bowel wall ischemia

Petersen and other hernias after gastric bypass are covered in the Postsurgical upper GI anatomy lesson.
